svg.title: One page of neural networks from scratch, drawn by hand
svg.desc: A hand-drawn single-sheet reference for the Neural Networks from Scratch series, laid out in eight panels. Panel one tables the forward pass in order, giving each stage its output shape for a batch of N samples: the input batch at N by 2, a Dense layer to N by 3, ReLU unchanged at N by 3, a second Dense layer producing logits, softmax producing rows that sum to one, and the loss collapsing to a scalar; it is headed by the rule that inner dimensions match and outer dimensions survive, and closes by noting that without a ReLU between them two Dense layers collapse into one. Panel two gives the four object kinds — Layer, Activation, Loss and Optimiser — each with its method contract and the state it owns, noting that two further classes fuse an activation with a loss, that swapping only the Loss turns the same stack into a regressor, and that a convolutional layer is still a forward and a backward while AdamW is still the same three optimiser hooks. Panel three gives the three gradients a Dense layer computes — dweights as the input transpose dotted with the upstream gradient, dbiases as a keepdims sum over the batch, dinputs as the upstream gradient dotted with the weight transpose — each with its shape, above the two fused backward passes, softmax with cross-entropy and sigmoid with binary cross-entropy, which both collapse to predictions minus targets over N; its subtitle records that random search moved the loss only from 1.099 to 1.095 in a hundred thousand draws, which is why gradients exist. Panel four lists six optimisers in the order the series builds them, each with its update rule, its characteristic hyperparameter and its measured accuracy and loss on one shared spiral run: SGD at 64.7 per cent and 0.87, decay at 64.7 and 0.76, momentum at 95.7 and 0.12, AdaGrad at 84.0 and 0.38, RMSProp at 90.0 and 0.24, and Adam at 96.3 and 0.08; it notes Adam's class defaults and that vanilla SGD is slow rather than stuck, reaching 90.7 per cent by fifty thousand epochs. Panel five runs the training loop in two lanes: lane A, the training step, scales inputs, batches, runs the forward pass with dropout on, computes the data and regularisation loss with a running accuracy tally, runs the backward pass and then the three optimiser hooks; lane B, evaluation, applies the stored scaling, runs forward with training set to false, takes the data loss only, takes an argmax and scores, differing from lane A only by subtraction. Panel six lists six ways training fails with each symptom and its first fix: dead ReLU, vanishing initialisation, overfitting, the AdaGrad stall, an optimiser rebuilt inside the loop, and dropout left on at evaluation. Panel seven reads the train-test gap, from underfitting through a good fit to overfitting, then gives L2, L1 and dropout with their measured effect on test accuracy. Panel eight sets five numerical-floor rules — subtract the row max before exponentiating, clip before taking a log, split the sigmoid on the sign of z, keep dimensions on every reduction, and the np.dot patch nnfs.init() installs — against five checks to run before trusting a training run, and observes that only the last rule raises anything while the rest fail silently. A footer records the four projects as run end to end: MNIST at 98.0 per cent, two-moons at 100, Fashion-MNIST at 87.1, and California housing at an R squared of 0.823. Same eight-panel rhythm as the Context Engineering poster, so the two can be read side by side.
svg.text: One page of neural networks from scratch
Everything the network computes on one pass, and everything that changes it on the way back.
Z₁ = X · W₁ + b₁, W₁ is (2, 3)
Z₂ = A₁ · W₂ + b₂, the logits
exp(Z₂ − rowmax) / Σ, rows sum to 1
−log ŷ at the true class, meaned
Without a ReLU between them, two Dense layers collapse into one.
One of four kinds, plus two that fuse an activation and a loss.
Layer_Dense owns weights, biases, and their gradients
Activation_ReLU: no parameters; inputs, output, dinputs
the base class adds calculate() and regularization_loss()
Optimizer_Adam keeps its buffers on the layer, not on itself
Swap the Loss and it regresses: project 04, Loss_MSE, no activation.
A conv layer is still a forward and a backward; AdamW, three hooks.
Random search moved the loss 1.099 → 1.095 in 100 000 draws.
one local derivative per function, multiplied
(1, n_out) — the bias input is always 1
(N, n_in) — sums the n_out paths each input feeds
(N, C) — O(N·C) work, not the O(N·C²) Jacobian
(N, 1) — ŷ(1−ŷ) cancels, so no tiny division
Every backward is the chain rule. The fused tail is (ŷ − y)/N.
One shared run: seed 0, spiral 300, 2→64→3, 10 001 epochs.
Adam defaults lr=0.001, decay=0, ε=1e-7, β₁=.9, β₂=.999; Part 27 runs .02.
Vanilla SGD is slow, not stuck: 64.7% at 10k epochs, 90.7% at 50k.
5 · The training loop, end to end
One step in two lanes. Lane B differs from lane A only by subtraction: no dropout, no regularisation loss, no backward, no update.
LANE A · TRAINING STEP · READS AND WRITES THE WEIGHTS
LANE B · EVALUATION · READS THEM AND NOTHING ELSE
Split 60–80 / 10–20 / 10–20. Tune on validation, refit, then open the test set once. k = 5 folds, each scaler refitted inside its fold.
B = 128 over 60 000 MNIST samples is 469 updates an epoch, 9 380 over twenty. Shuffle every epoch, and decay now applies per step.
The symptom as it appears, then the first thing to change.
gradients all zero; the unit outputs 0 for any input
first fix — He init sqrt(2/n_in), and lower the rate
loss flat at ln(C); variance ÷150 per layer at n=64
first fix — L2 5e-4 on dense1: test 84.0%, gap 11.3
the rate decays to zero and training stalls for good
first fix — RMSProp's decaying cache instead
Adam quietly degrades to plain SGD
first fix — build it once, outside both loops
test accuracy wanders from run to run
first fix — forward(x, training=False) at evaluation
The gap is the diagnosis. Figures below: 100 samples per class.
train low, test low, and a small gap
more neurons, more layers, more epochs
train high, test high, and a small gap
ship it, then watch for distribution shift
sparse; test 80.3%. L1+L2 gives the smallest gap, 1.7
8 · The numerical floor, and what to check before trusting a run
Only the last rule on the left raises anything. The other four just make the numbers quietly wrong.
1 · Subtract the per-row max before np.exp, or e¹⁰⁰⁰ = inf.
3 · Split the sigmoid on the sign of z; np.exp overflows past 700.
4 · keepdims=True on every reduction, or (N,) broadcasts as a row.
5 · nnfs.init() patches np.dot; a plain Python list raises.
Gradient-check: centred difference h=1e-5, rel. error < 1e-5.
assert dweights.shape == weights.shape, on every layer.
Overfit one tiny batch first; scale up once it reaches 100%.
Post-ReLU zero fraction near 0.5, activation std near 1.
Four projects, run end to end — MNIST 98.0% · two-moons 100% · Fashion-MNIST 87.1% · California housing R² 0.823, RMSE $49.2k.
Neural Networks from Scratch — 35 posts, 4 projects, NumPy only. Every figure here is measured under nnfs.init() seed 0, not assumed.
